theme: Jerusalem falls; the exile, covenant curses fulfilled
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 24:1-25:30. This is the end of the kingdom of Judah. Read it as the fulfillment of the covenant curses you saw in Deuteronomy, and look for the small sign of hope in the last verses.
settingTheScene: After Josiah’s death, Judah’s last four kings ruled for about twenty-three years under the shadow of Egypt and Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar took the first exiles, including Daniel and Ezekiel, in 605 and 597 BC. The final siege ended in 586 BC, when Jerusalem and the temple were burned. This chapter is the historical backdrop for all the prophets you will read in this unit.
observation: “Surely this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD, to remove them out of his sight” (24:3).
Nebuchadnezzar carried off “all Jerusalem… ten thousand captives” in 597 BC (24:14).
Zedekiah “rebelled against the king of Babylon” (24:20).
“On the seventh day of the fifth month… Nebuzaradan… burned the house of the LORD and the king’s house and all the houses of Jerusalem” (25:8-9).
They killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes and then blinded him (25:7).
The bronze pillars, the sea, and the temple vessels were broken up and carried to Babylon (25:13-17).
“So Judah was taken into exile out of its land” (25:21).
“Evil-merodach king of Babylon… graciously freed Jehoiachin from prison… and Jehoiachin dined regularly at the king’s table” (25:27-29).
interpretation:
The story is told with terrible plainness. The writer does not shout or linger. He lists the steps: the siege, the famine, the breach in the wall, the flight of the king, the burning of the temple, the stripping of the bronze, the deportation. The curses of Deuteronomy 28 have come true in order. The nation that was brought out of Egypt is carried back into foreign captivity.

The blame is placed squarely on Judah’s sin, and especially Manasseh’s. But the Lord is the one who sends the Babylonians. This is a point the prophets will make again and again: Babylon is God’s instrument, not his master. Exile is not a sign that God lost. It is a sign that God keeps his word.

Notice the loss of everything that Judah trusted in. The temple is destroyed, which they believed could never fall. The king is blinded and bound. The land is emptied. The articles of worship are melted down. There is nothing left to stand on except God himself.

And then the last four verses. After thirty-seven years in prison, Jehoiachin, the king of David’s line, is released and given a seat at Babylon’s table. It is a small thing. But it shows that David’s line is not extinct. The promise of 2 Samuel 7 has not been cancelled. The writer ends the book with a candle in the dark, and the prophets will light more.
connection: Matthew 1:11-12 includes the exile in the genealogy of Jesus: “Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon.” Jesus predicted another fall of Jerusalem (Luke 21:20-24), and Hebrews 12:27-28 speaks of a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Romans 11:22 pairs God’s kindness and severity. Lamentations will give voice to this grief in a few days.
application:
Take a moment to sit with the weight of this chapter. Judgment is real, and God means what he says.

Ask what you have trusted in as unshakeable: a building, a position, a routine. Where does your security come from?

Remember the small candle at the end, and look for small signs of God’s faithfulness in dark times.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to fear him and not presume on his patience.
Ask him to hold you when everything is lost.
Thank him that he keeps his word in judgment and mercy.
